**Abstract** — The survival and growth of early-stage technology startups depend heavily on their ability to attract tech workers. It is popular for startups to offer stock options to rank-and-file tech workers, a practice rooted in the financial view that the financial prospects associated with these offerings help attract employees. Yet, recent research suggests tech workers often lack the knowledge necessary to properly evaluate stock options, casting doubt on this justification. To this end, we conducted a series of experiments to examine whether, and why, startup stock options may attract tech workers. We find a strong employee attraction effect for startups that offer stock options, which however is only partially driven by financial considerations. **Abstract** — Abstract Research Summary Evaluating early‐stage ventures is difficult because observable signals of future quality are weak and noisy. How closely are evaluators' assessments related to venture quality, and do their subjective judgments add to the information already available about a venture? Using more than 1600 screening decisions from a venture incubator, we examine how judges use application information to evaluate ventures by rating them on a set of 14 criteria and providing an overall recommendation. Judges' beliefs as recorded in the grades of the criteria explain their recommendations well, but they are only weakly associated with venture quality. ### 3 · Spatial (In)equality and Entrepreneurial Ecosystem Policy: A Historical Analysis of the Scottish Highlands

| | |
|---|---|
| **📰 Journal** | Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice (ETP) |
| **👤 Authors** | Shannon Harris · Mia Clarke · Anna Brattström |
| **📅 Published** | 2026-08-25 |
| **🏷️ Tags** | `FT50` `Innovation-Core` |
| **🔗 DOI** | [10.1177/10422587261472141](https://doi.org/10.1177/10422587261472141) |

**Abstract** — We built a theory on how entrepreneurial ecosystem policy benefits some places within rural regions while leaving others behind. In a historical analysis of the Scottish Highlands and Islands, 1965 to 1990, we compared policies that attract external resources from outside the region with those that embed resources within local communities. We found that resource-attracting policies not only generated higher economic output but also concentrated opportunity, drained peripheral areas, and increased regional fragility. Resource-embedding policies produced lower aggregate output but greater spatial inclusion and resilience. Our historical analysis identifies spatial draining, disempowerment, and empowerment as mechanisms through which policy shapes ecosystem outcomes over time.

**Topics:** `Rural development and sustainability` `Regional resilience and development` `Regional Development and Policy`

</td></tr></table>

**Abstract** — The Occupational Information Network (O*NET) is a database of occupational descriptors sponsored by the U.S. Department of Labor. Since its release around the turn of the century, O*NET has taken on a broad and important role in management and organizational research as a key data source for occupational characteristics. It is common practice for researchers to combine or adapt descriptors from O*NET’s content model to measure constructs that O*NET does not capture directly (e.g., job complexity, emotional labor demands). ### 8 · A Process Model of Managerial Phronesis in the Age of Generative AI

| | |
|---|---|
| **📰 Journal** | Academy of Management Review (AMR) |
| **👤 Authors** | Dirk Lindebaum · Natarajan Balasubramanian · Mehreen Ashraf · Patrick Haack |
| **📅 Published** | 2026-08-25 |
| **🏷️ Tags** | `FT50` `UTD24` `Innovation-Core` |
| **🔗 DOI** | [10.5465/amr.2024.0582](https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2024.0582) |

**Abstract** — Managerial phronesis involves first-hand experience that helps managers make moral and context-specific judgments at work in pursuit of the common good. Yet, as managers increasingly rely on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) at work, many of these first-hand experiences are replaced by synthetic outputs.
